native_result.query: How were the phases of the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE) characterized in terms of the first principal component in a PCA on the forms of capital analyzed in hundred-year time slices?
native_result.HypoA: During the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE), both phases are primarily associated with negative values on the first principal component (PC1). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.
native_result.HypoB: In a PCA of the 12 forms-of-capital indicators analysed in 100-year slices (PC1, ~30% of variance, a balanced composite of all four capital dimensions with strongest positive loadings on copper/gold, pottery decoration, depots and weapons and negative loadings on pottery form, axes/celts and amber), the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) is characterised by a net decline in PC1 (from -0.58 to -1.78, about -1.2 standard deviations, with a brief rebound around 3100 BCE), while the Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE) is characterised by a net recovery (from -1.50 to -0.41, about +1.1 SD, dip in the early/mid phase and a sharp rise at 2300 BCE), returning the capital composite to roughly its 3400 BCE level by the end of the Younger Neolithic.
native_result.WorkflowB: Parsed capital.csv (decimal commas to float; dropped group/color); global z-score standardisation (ddof=1) of the 12 Z-variables across all 39 100-year bins; SVD-based PCA with PC1 sign fixed so loadings sum positive; extracted per-bin PC1 scores, loadings and explained variance; robustness check via PCA on raw values (corr 0.997); cross-check by independently binning the annual time_series_data.csv into 100-year means and repeating the PCA (same directional pattern).

sub_hypo.text: The Middle Neolithic (3400–3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900–2300 BCE) are both primarily associated with negative PC1 values in a PCA using individual forms-of-capital values as attributes.
sub_hypo.context: Forms of capital during the Middle Neolithic (3400–3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900–2300 BCE).
sub_hypo.relations: Both chronological phases are primarily associated with negative scores on PC1 derived from a PCA whose attributes are the individual forms-of-capital values.

gold_sub_hypo.full_hypo: During the Middle Neolithic (3400-3000 BCE) and Younger Neolithic (2900-2300 BCE), both phases are primarily associated with negative values on the first principal component (PC1). This Principal component analysis (PCA) is on the forms of capital. The values of the individual elements of the forms of capital form the attributes.

sub_hypo.text: PC1 of the 12 forms-of-capital indicators explains approximately 30% of variance and is a balanced composite of all four capital dimensions, with the strongest positive loadings on copper/gold, pottery decoration, depots and weapons, and negative loadings on pottery form, axes/celts and amber.
sub_hypo.context: Archaeological capital indicators in 39 100-year bins; globally z-score standardised (ddof=1), with SVD-based PCA and PC1 sign fixed so its loadings sum positive.
sub_hypo.relations: PC1 explains approximately 30% of variance; its strongest positive loadings are on copper/gold, pottery decoration, depots and weapons, while pottery form, axes/celts and amber load negatively.

sub_hypo.text: During the Middle Neolithic (3400–3000 BCE), the capital PC1 composite declines from -0.58 to -1.78, approximately -1.2 standard deviations, with a brief rebound around 3100 BCE.
sub_hypo.context: Middle Neolithic, 3400–3000 BCE, analysed in 100-year slices using PC1 from globally standardised capital indicators.
sub_hypo.relations: The derived PC1 score shows a net temporal decline from -0.58 to -1.78, interrupted by a brief rebound around 3100 BCE.

sub_hypo.text: During the Younger Neolithic (2900–2300 BCE), the capital PC1 composite recovers from -1.50 to -0.41, approximately +1.1 standard deviations, with an early/mid-phase dip and a sharp rise at 2300 BCE, returning roughly to its 3400 BCE level.
sub_hypo.context: Younger Neolithic, 2900–2300 BCE, analysed in 100-year slices using PC1 from globally standardised capital indicators, with comparison to 3400 BCE.
sub_hypo.relations: The derived PC1 score shows a net temporal recovery from -1.50 to -0.41 despite an early/mid-phase dip, rising sharply at 2300 BCE; the final score is roughly comparable to -0.58 at 3400 BCE.
